newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian police, demonstrators end stand-off.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian police, demonstrators end stand-off.

text.p: Indonesian security forces fired repeated rounds of tear gas and shots in the air to disperse followers of a minority party during a campaign march on Saturday through an eastern district of Jakarta, witnesses said.

They said thousands of supporters of the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) hurled stones and chanted slogans as they tried to force their way into a street blocked off by police in Jati Negara district.
Witnesses said police fired tear gas and rubber bullets and then shot into the air after the march threatened to turn more violent.
The protesters regrouped after a while, but police finally managed to clear the area after some three hours of intermittent street battles, witnesses said.
An official at the scene said one soldier backing up police had received a head wound from a stone.
But another senior police officer said there were no injuries or arrests. He said the only damage in the clash was to one car parked in the area, which had its windows shattered.
Demonstrators burned flags of the ruling Golkar party, in power for the last 30 years, and ripped down other Golkar banners before dispersing.
The PPP supporters complained that Golkar followers had been allowed to parade through the blocked off street.
The PPP, Golkar and the minority Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) are the only three parties legally entitled to contest Indonesia's May 29 national and local elections.

The three parties agreed before the contest started for the May 29 polls to campaign in separate areas each day to avoid violent confrontations. Saturday was PPP's day on Java, the country's most populated island with some 60 percent of the Indonesian population of 200 million.
In Jakarta, many shops were closed during the day for fear that PPP campaigning would turn violent and there was little traffic on the street other than the party's supporters.
Golkar is guaranteed a comfortable victory and is seeking just over 70 percent of the vote from the 125 million electorate. The PPP is giving Golkar its strongest challenge.

Most of the violence since the campaign for 425 elected seats in the House of Representatves opened on April 27 has been restricted to central Java. The other 75 seats in the house are reserved for the military which does not vote.

Armed forces (ABRI) spokesman Brigadier-General Slamet Supriadi was quoted in the Jakarta Post on Saturday as saying that as of Thursday, 73 people had died during the campaign - most of them in traffic accidents.
"ABRI has made an all out effort to maintain security," he added.

Reuters correspondent Lewa Pardomuan reported from central Java that troops were on guard in the town of Parakan, where thousands of people claiming to be PPP supporters had rioted on Wednesday, ransacking banks and shops.

The riot erupted during a 10 km (six mile) march by some 6,000 PPP supporters in protest against what they said was government bias in favour of the ruling Golkar and beatings they said the PPP had suffered in the hands of security authorities.

"We are all scared here. We don't dare to fully open our shops because violence may erupt at any time," said a shop owner in the hilly town of 200,000 set amid tobacco plantations near the ancient city of Yogyakarta.
"This town is usually crowded, especially on Saturday. It's quiet now because people are afraid of the election. The PPP rallies always make us scared," a woman vegetable seller said.
